'''''Pouteria campechiana''''' (commonly known as the '''cupcake fruit''', '''eggfruit''', '''zapote amarillo''', '''yellow sapote''' or '''canistel''') is an [[evergreen]] tree native to, and cultivated in, southern Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and El Salvador.<ref>{{GRIN | access-date=2009-01-29 }}</ref> It is cultivated in other countries, such as India, Costa Rica, Brazil, the United States, the Dominican Republic, Australia, Cambodia,<ref name="Lim">{{cite book |pages=133–134 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_a9EAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA134 |title=Edible Medicinal And Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 6, Fruits |author=T. K. Lim |year=2013 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-007-5628-1 }}</ref> Vietnam, Taiwan, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Nigeria, Cameroon and the Philippines. The edible part of the tree is its fruit, which is colloquially known as an '''egg fruit'''.<ref name="Lim"/>

The canistel grows up to {{cvt|10|m|ft|0}} high, and produces orange-yellow fruit up to {{cvt|7|cm|in|0}} long, which are edible raw. Canistel flesh is sweet, with a texture often compared to that of a [[Boiled egg#Hard-boiled eggs|hard-boiled egg yolk]], hence its colloquial name "eggfruit". It is closely related to the [[lúcuma]], [[mamey sapote]], and [[abiu]].

==Fruit description==
The shape and size of the fruit is highly variable, depending on the cultivar. The better selections consistently produce large, ovate fruit with glossy skin weighing upwards of 400 g (14 oz). The flesh is somewhat pasty, although the best varieties have a creamy, mousse-like texture. The flavor is rich and is reminiscent of an egg custard.<ref>{{cite book |author=Charles Boning |title=Florida's Best Fruiting Plants: Native and Exotic Trees, Shrubs, and Vines |year=2006 |publisher=Pineapple Press, Inc. |location=Sarasota, Florida |page=53 }}</ref> The fruit may contain one to six large, brown seeds.

The canistel is a [[Climacteric (botany)|climacteric]] fruit, so it continues to ripen after harvest. A fully mature fruit shows an intense yellow skin color. Eventually, it softens and drops from the tree. Insects and birds avoid the fruit, perhaps due to its [[astringent]] properties. The bitterness is perceptible to the human palate as well, though much reduced as the fruit overripens. Mature fruits harvested while hard may not ripen properly: the fruits may remain astringent and fail to develop its signature texture reminiscent of egg yolk.

==Uses==
Like the related [[lúcuma]], the canistel can be eaten fresh, and has the texture of a hard-boiled egg yolk.<ref name="Lim"/> The ripe fruit can be made into jam, marmalade, pancakes, and flour.<ref name=lavulu/> The ripe flesh is blended with milk and other ingredients to make a shake, and pureed, it is sometimes added to custards or used in making ice cream.<ref name=Morton>{{cite book |title=Fruits of Warm Climates |author=Julia F. Morton |author-link=Julia Morton |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/canistel.html |year=1987 |chapter=Canistel |pages=402–405 |access-date=2010-09-24 |archive-date=2023-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230821085044/https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/canistel.html |url-status=live }}</ref> It is also used in a milkshake known as "eggfruit nog".<ref name="Lim"/>

The wood of the tree is occasionally used in construction where it is available, especially as planks or rafters. In its native range, it has been a source of latex used to adulterate [[chicle]].<ref name=Morton/>

==Etymology==
Its [[binomial name|specific name]] is derived from the Mexican town of [[Campeche, Campeche|Campeche]], where it is native.

In the numerous countries where it is cultivated or sold, it is known by many vernacular names; canistel is common, as are variations on egg fruit and names referring to its yellow color.<ref name="Lim2013">{{cite book |author=Tong Kwee Lim |title=Edible Medicinal And Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 6, Fruits |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_a9EAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA134 |date=15 February 2013 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-94-007-5628-1 |page=134 }}</ref> In the Philippines, it is called ''chesa'', ''tiessa'', or ''atiesa''. In Sri Lanka, this fruit is known as ''lavul'', ''laulu'', ''lavulu'', or ''lawalu''.<ref name=lavulu>{{cite book |url=http://www.worldagroforestry.org/downloads/publications/PDFs/BC07321.PDF |chapter=Lavulu |author=D.K.N.G. Pushpakumara |title=Underutilized fruit trees in Sri Lanka |year=2007 |publisher=World Agroforestry Centre, South Asia Office, New Delhi, India |archive-date=2017-07-13 |access-date=2011-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713121243/http://www.worldagroforestry.org/downloads/Publications/PDFS/BC07321.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In Thailand, it is known by different traditional popular names such as {{lang|th-Latn|lamut Khamen}} ({{lang|th|ละมุดเขมร}}="Khmer sapodilla") or {{lang|th-Latn|tho Khamen}} ({{lang|th|ท้อเขมร}}="Khmer peach"), folk imagination attributing a hypothetical Cambodian origin to this fruit (the name of the fruit is ''see da'' in Cambodia).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://thaimisc.pukpik.com/freewebboard/php/vreply.php?user=maipradab3&topic=4851 |title=มีเมล็ดละมุดเขมรหรือเซียนท้อจำหน่าย |access-date=2012-08-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160531154415/http://thaimisc.pukpik.com/freewebboard/php/vreply.php?user=maipradab3&topic=4851 |archive-date=2016-05-31 }}</ref> Currently, those names are discouraged by linguistic authorities and names making no reference to Cambodia, such as ''tiesa'' (ทิสซา), are officially favored.<ref name="7Benefits">{{Cite web |url=http://www.greenerald.com/%E0%B8%A1%E0%B9%88%E0%B8%AD%E0%B8%99%E0%B9%84%E0%B8%82%E0%B9%88/ |title=7 Health Benefits of Canistel |access-date=2020-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140327130307/http://www.greenerald.com/%e0%b8%a1%e0%b9%88%e0%b8%ad%e0%b8%99%e0%b9%84%e0%b8%82%e0%b9%88/ |archive-date=2014-03-27 }}</ref>

The fruit is also given names after its unique yellow colour similar to an [[egg yolk]]: it is known as the {{lang|ms|buah kuning telur}} ("yolk fruit") in Malay,<ref name="Exotic Fruits">{{cite book |author1=Fadzilah Awang-Kanak |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780128031384/exotic-fruits |title=Exotic Fruits Reference Guide |author2=Mohd Fadzelly Abu Bakar |publisher=Academic Press |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-12-803138-4 |editor-last=Rodrigues |editor-first=Sueli |pages=107–111 |chapter=Canistel - ''Pouteria campechiana'' |editor-last2=de Oliveira Silva |editor-first2=Ebenezer |editor-last3=de Brito |editor-first3=Edy Sousa |archive-date=2021-06-24 |access-date=2021-06-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624204449/https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780128031384/exotic-fruits |url-status=live }}</ref> {{lang|vi|cây trứng gà}} ("chicken egg plant") in Vietnamese, {{lang|th-Latn|mon khai}} ({{lang|th|ม่อนไข่}}, {{lang|th-Latn|khai}} meaning "egg") in Thai,<ref name="7Benefits" /> and ''danhuang guo'' ({{lang|zh|蛋黃果}} "egg yolk fruit") in Taiwan.

It is called ''sawo mentega'' ("butter sapodilla", for its color and texture) throughout Southeast Asia.<ref name="Exotic Fruits" /> It is also known as ''alkesah'' in Indonesia.

Though relatively rare in East Africa, they can be found, and in the [[Swahili language]], the fruit is confusingly named {{lang|sw|zaituni}}, which is the same word used to refer to [[olives]].

The Taiwanese also call this fruit ''xiantao'' ({{lang|zh|仙桃}}), "peach of the [[Xian (Taoism)|immortal]]s".
